title: Life Together: Humility, Care, and Forgiveness
summary: When the disciples ask who is greatest, Jesus sets a child among them and teaches humility, warns severely against causing little ones to stumble, and tells of a shepherd who searches for one lost sheep. He gives steps for dealing with a brother who sins, promising his presence where two or three gather in his name. To Peter's question about how often to forgive, he answers with the parable of a servant forgiven a vast debt who refuses to forgive a small one.
story: Having taught his disciples that he must suffer (16:21 and 17:22-23), Jesus now teaches them how to live together as his community while they wait for what is coming. This is the fourth of Matthew's five great discourses, sometimes called the community discourse, and it follows the promise that Jesus will build his church (16:18). Its setting in Capernaum is private: the audience is the disciples, not the crowds. The chapter moves from status to care to discipline to forgiveness, and each section corrects a natural instinct. The disciples ask about greatness; Jesus answers with a child. They might count how often to forgive; Jesus answers with a debt no one could repay.
historical:
The chapter's instructions for dealing with sin in the community draw on the law of Moses: Deuteronomy 19:15 required two or three witnesses to establish a charge, and Leviticus 19:17 commanded Israelites to rebuke a neighbor frankly rather than hate him in their hearts. Jewish communities of the period had procedures of their own; the Dead Sea Scrolls, from a community near Qumran, describe members reproving one another before witnesses before bringing a matter to the assembly. Jesus' word church (ekklesia) in verse 17 may refer to a local gathering of his followers, and Matthew's first readers would have heard it as instructions for their own congregations.

The parable's sums would have stunned hearers. A talent was the largest unit of money, equal to about six thousand denarii, and a denarius was roughly a day's wage for a laborer. Ten thousand talents, using the largest Greek number and the largest unit, is a deliberately impossible amount. Josephus records that the yearly revenue of Herod Antipas's whole territory of Galilee and Perea was two hundred talents. The fellow servant's debt of a hundred denarii, about four months' wages, was real money but trivial by comparison. The parallels are Mark 9:33-50 for the teaching on greatness and stumbling, Luke 15:3-7 for the lost sheep (told there in answer to critics), and Luke 17:1-4 for forgiveness.
cultural:
Children in the ancient world had little status. They were loved, but they had no rights, no achievements, and no standing to claim. To become like a child is to stop jockeying for rank and to depend on another. The millstone in verse 6 is literally a donkey's millstone, the large upper stone of a mill turned by an animal, far heavier than the hand mills used at home. Drowning with such a stone was a horror, partly because a body lost at sea received no burial.

Shepherds counted their sheep at the end of each day, and leaving ninety-nine in open country to search for one reflects the value of each animal and the shepherd's responsibility. Selling a debtor with his wife and children into slavery was an accepted, if harsh, way of recovering losses in the ancient world (compare 2 Kings 4:1), and a debtor could be imprisoned until relatives paid. Tax collectors and pagans (Gentiles) in verse 17 were people outside the community of Israel. Peter's offer to forgive seven times, the number of completeness, would have seemed generous. Jesus' answer, seventy-seven times (the Greek can also be read as seventy times seven), echoes Lamech's boast in Genesis 4:24 that he would be avenged seventy-sevenfold, reversing the song of limitless revenge into limitless forgiveness.
literary: The discourse has two halves, each opened by a question (verses 1 and 21) and each ending with a word about the Father in heaven (verses 14 and 35). The first half concerns the little ones: humility (verses 1 to 5), not causing them to stumble (verses 6 to 9), and seeking them when they stray (verses 10 to 14). The second half concerns the brother who sins: correction (verses 15 to 20) and forgiveness (verses 21 to 35). The two halves balance each other. The community must pursue those who wander and confront those who sin, but it must always forgive. The hyperbole of verses 8 and 9, cutting off a hand or tearing out an eye, is a vivid way of saying that nothing is worth keeping if it leads to sin; it is not a command to self-harm. Verse 11 in later manuscripts repeats Luke 19:10 and is absent from the earliest ones. The discourse ends with the formula of 19:1, when Jesus had finished these sayings.

outline.t: The greatest in the kingdom: become like a child
Warnings against causing others to stumble
When a brother sins: correction and restoration
How often to forgive: the unforgiving servant

doctrines.note: This chapter is Jesus' instruction for his community. It is marked by humility rather than rank, protective care for the vulnerable, patient correction aimed at restoring rather than punishing, and the presence of Jesus himself where two or three gather in his name.

The forgiven debt in the parable pictures God's grace: a debt that could never be repaid, cancelled out of compassion. That grace is meant to reshape the forgiven, so that mercy received becomes mercy given.

The chapter takes sin seriously in both directions: causing others to stumble brings a fearful woe, and one's own sin must be cut away at any cost. Yet the aim in dealing with sin is always to win the brother back.

words.note: Skandalon, a trap or stumbling block, something that trips a person into falling. The related verb appears in verses 6, 8, and 9. The chapter's concern is not minor offense but causing someone to fall away from faith, especially someone vulnerable.

Tapeinoo, to make low or humble. To humble oneself like a child is to take the low place willingly. Matthew uses the adjective from the same family for Jesus, who is humble (tapeinos) in heart (11:29): the greatest in the kingdom resemble the king.

Hebdomekontakis, seventy times. With seven it can be read as seventy-seven or seventy times seven; the Greek Old Testament of Genesis 4:24 uses the same phrase for Lamech's vengeance, which favors seventy-seven. Either way, the point is that forgiveness is not to be counted.

Talanton, talent, originally a unit of weight and then the largest unit of money, worth about six thousand denarii. Ten thousand talents is a figure meant to be beyond comprehension, like the debt of sin before God.

christ: Jesus speaks here as the Lord of his church, promising to be present among his gathered people in a way that echoes Jewish teaching about God's presence resting among those who study the law together, and the promise of 1:23 that he is Immanuel, God with us. The parable of the lost sheep reflects the shepherd of Ezekiel 34, where God himself promises to seek the lost and bring back the strayed, and Jesus embodies that search in his ministry to tax collectors and sinners. The parable of the unforgiving servant pictures the grace Jesus brings: the king's cancellation of an unpayable debt anticipates the cross, where Jesus gives his blood “for the forgiveness of sins” (26:28). Jesus himself becomes the model of the humility he commends, the greatest who took the lowest place.

hard.q: Does God's forgiveness depend on our forgiving others?
hard.a: Verse 35 is stark: the Father will treat the unforgiving as the king treated the servant, handing him over until he repays. It echoes 6:14-15, where Jesus says that if we do not forgive others, the Father will not forgive us. This seems to make forgiveness depend on our performance, which would conflict with the grace the parable itself describes. Most interpreters answer by noting the parable's order: the king forgives first, freely and completely, before the servant does anything. The servant's refusal to forgive shows that the mercy he received never changed him; he treated the king's pardon as a lucky escape rather than a gift that reshapes the heart. On this reading, forgiving others is not the price of God's forgiveness but the evidence that it has been received. Different traditions frame the relationship differently, some stressing the unity of faith and its fruit, others the ongoing necessity of forgiving as part of remaining in grace, but all agree that a person who clings to unforgiveness is in spiritual danger. The parable also does not require pretending a wrong did not happen, avoiding the correction described in verses 15 to 17, or remaining in danger from an abuser; forgiveness releases the debt, but it does not erase the truth or the need for safety and repentance.

questions: Jesus answered a question about greatness by pointing to a child. Where do you find yourself caring about rank or status among other Christians?
Jesus lays out steps for confronting a brother privately first. Why do you think we so often skip the first step and talk to others instead?
Think of the debt you have been forgiven. Is there someone whose smaller debt to you you are still holding onto?
